title: Gameweek 1's Biggest Fantasy Surprises
dek: Five players who blew past PitchMetric's predicted points in the season's opening round — and why a Gameweek 1 model has almost nothing to go on.
intro: Every player here cleared 30 minutes on the pitch in Gameweek 1, which leaves 229 qualifying performances to rank by one number: actual points scored minus PitchMetric's predicted points (xP) for that player, that match. The five below are the biggest positive gaps of the round — the players the model most under-rated. A shared theme runs through all five, and it's a real limitation, not a bug: Gameweek 1 is the one week of the season where the model's per-player scoring rates (goal share, assist share) have literally zero current-season data to draw on, since nobody has a start yet when the predictions are made. It falls back to a flat appearance-and-clean-sheet floor for almost everyone, which means it's structurally blind to exactly the kind of breakout individual moments that decide fantasy gameweeks. See the methodology for the full model.
closing: Four of these five points came out of just two matches — Brighton's and Hull City's, both wins built on a clean sheet plus a goal from an unheralded name. That's the Gameweek 1 pattern in miniature: the model correctly rates a fixture's clean-sheet chance, but has no way yet to know which individual will supply the goal on top of it. From Gameweek 2 onward, every one of these players now has a real observed data point, and the model's individual rates stop being flat — see how that plays out in Gameweek 2's surprise list.

players.name: Maxim De Cuyper
players.analysis: The single biggest surprise of the round, in either direction. A left-back with zero registered minutes for the model to price entered Gameweek 1 as a flat 1.53 xP — appearance points and a share of Brighton's clean-sheet probability, nothing else — and left a 4-0 rout of Aston Villa with a goal, an assist, a clean sheet and two bonus points. It wasn't a fluke on the underlying numbers either: 1.47 expected goals and 0.21 expected assists (1.68 combined) means the chances he actually got were genuinely high-quality, not scraps. That's the sharpest illustration of Gameweek 1's blind spot — the model had no way to know this specific fixture would funnel that much of Brighton's attacking output through their left-back.

players.name: Jack Hinshelwood
players.analysis: Brighton's second Gameweek 1 shock, from the same 4-0 win over Aston Villa as De Cuyper above — a home academy product who came off after 63 minutes with a brace, the game's top bonus haul, and 1.41 expected goals backing up the finishing. Predicted xP was 1.56, essentially the same generic floor every outfield player without a scoring history got that week. Two Brighton players this high on the same list, from the same clean sheet, says more about how little the model could differentiate within a squad in Gameweek 1 than it does about either player individually.

players.name: Nobel Mendy
players.analysis: Hull City beat Manchester United 2-0 on their return to the Premier League, and Mendy was one of two home defenders who scored in it — a top-flight debut the model had precisely nothing to go on beyond a generic clean-sheet floor of 1.83 xP. His goal came from a shot worth only 0.28 expected goals — a low-probability strike rather than a tap-in, which makes the outcome as much a one-off as a repeatable signal. No free-licensed photo of Nobel Mendy is available on Wikimedia Commons yet.

players.name: Semi Ajayi
players.analysis: The second of two Hull City center-backs to score in that 2-0 win over Manchester United — same clean sheet as Mendy above, same 1.83 xP floor, a different goal (0.52 expected goals this time, a somewhat more presentable chance). A club with literally no 2026-27 track record produced two double-digit defensive returns from sixty-three shared minutes against one of the league's biggest names, which is exactly the kind of team-level outcome a fixture model can flag as "clean sheet likely" without any way to say which two names would cash it in.

players.name: Mamadou Sangaré
players.analysis: Two assists and a clean sheet in a 3-0 win over Spurs, from a midfielder the model had priced at a flat 1.95 xP. His 0.33 expected assists is the most encouraging underlying number on this list relative to the actual return — genuine chance creation, not just a stat-line that happened to him. Worth revisiting once he has a body of current-season data behind him rather than a blank slate.

title: Gameweek 2's Biggest Fantasy Surprises
dek: A Bruno Fernandes hat-trick headlines the round, but the more interesting story is what changed in the model's own inputs one gameweek in.
intro: Same method as Gameweek 1 — every player below played at least 30 minutes, and is ranked by actual points minus PitchMetric's predicted xP for that fixture. The difference this time is that the model is no longer working from a blank slate: every returning player now has one gameweek of real 2026-27 output behind their goal and assist rates, and it shows in who tops this list and why. See the methodology for exactly how a player's rate is computed from real per-match history rather than an assumption.
closing: Compare the underlying expected-goals numbers across this list and two different stories emerge. Bruno Fernandes's 2.02 xG very nearly explains his hat-trick outright — his performance was mostly signal, a genuine chance-quality outburst the model just had no prior data to anticipate. Haaland (0.66 xG for two goals) and Groß (0.05 xG for a goal) leaned much more on finishing than on chance quality — closer to variance than to a repeatable pattern. Rayan Cherki's case is different again: the model actively discounted him (start probability capped at 0.3) for having zero starts to his name after Gameweek 1, which was reasonable caution right up until he played 81 minutes and scored twice. None of that is a flaw exactly — it's what a model honestly built from observed history looks like in only its second week of data.

players.name: Bruno Fernandes
players.analysis: The biggest single surprise across both gameweeks. A blank Gameweek 1 left his model-computed goal and assist rate at zero going into this fixture, so predicted xP stayed near the generic floor at 2.14 even though he's United's most expensive midfielder. What actually happened was a hat-trick plus an assist in a 5-2 win over Ipswich Town — and 2.02 expected goals means the underlying chances very nearly justify the goal tally on their own. This is the good kind of model miss: not a fluke the numbers can't explain, just one match of real data that hadn't happened yet when the prediction was made.

players.name: Rayan Cherki
players.analysis: The lowest predicted score in either week's top five, and for a specific, defensible reason: zero starts in Gameweek 1 capped his start probability at just 0.3 in the model, treating him as a fringe squad player rather than someone likely to see the pitch. He then played 81 minutes away at Crystal Palace, in a match City won 4-1, and scored twice. The 0.35 expected goals behind those two finishes says this was more clinical finishing than a string of clear-cut chances — the kind of return that's genuinely hard to have seen coming from where the data stood a week ago.

players.name: Morgan Gibbs-White
players.analysis: A goal and an assist away at Liverpool, in a match that finished 2-2, worth 13 points against a 1.72 prediction. The 0.79 expected goals behind his own finish is a reasonable, presentable chance rather than a wild outlier — the assist is the bigger surprise, with only 0.04 expected assists suggesting the pass that created it wasn't a high-probability chance-creation moment by the underlying numbers.

players.name: Erling Haaland
players.analysis: The most expensive player on either list, and still a double-digit surprise — his own blank Gameweek 1 left the model with no observed scoring rate to work from, so even the game's most reliable finisher started from a generic 2.17 xP floor. Two goals away at Crystal Palace, in the same 4-1 win as Cherki above, from just 0.66 combined expected goals is a big finishing overperformance on the underlying chances, not a case where the model missed obviously high-quality opportunities.

players.name: Pascal Groß
players.analysis: Brighton conceded four goals away at Chelsea and lost 4-3, but Groß personally returned a goal and an assist worth 13 points on his own. The 0.05 expected goals behind that goal is about as low as the underlying numbers get for an actual finish — the kind of moment a box score just can't explain, whatever it looked like on the pitch. The highest of this week's five predicted scores (2.60 xP, reflecting a track record as an established creative outlet) still wasn't close to enough.
